schools.summary: Keil sets the scene after six years of hiding and reads the account beside the fuller Kings narrative; Ellicott parses 'strengthened himself' and the Chronicler's added captain-names as his characteristic style.
Matthew Henry turns the notice into a hymn of restored providence and draws Jehoiada in five strokes — prudence, interest, faith, religion, resolution.
Clarke lays out the chapter's course and refers the reader to the parallel at 2 Kings 11:4.

Ellicott marks vv.2-3 as the Chronicler's own addition, the Levites' role absent from Kings, defending the fuller record as supplement not invention; Keil reads the gathering as the first stage of a carefully laid plan.
Ellicott identifies the covenanting parties, renders the priest's words as an acclamation, and grounds 'as the LORD hath said' in Nathan's oracle (2 Samuel 7).
Henry makes the divine entail of the crown the spring of Jehoiada's faith — 'the king's son must reign, as the Lord hath said.'

themes: the covenant in the house of God

schools.summary: Ellicott weighs the Chronicler's added 'priests and Levites' against the guardsmen of Kings, defending him from the charge of arbitrary alteration; Keil follows Bertheau's reconstruction of the three bands of the guard.

Ellicott fixes the gate of the foundation (the Sur of Kings) and reads 'all the people in the courts' as the strict legalist's reserve of the holy house to the priests; Keil identifies the Levite-guards and equates the death-penalty clause with Kings.
Wesley locates the gate of the foundation as the lower east gate at the foot of the steps from palace to temple.

Ellicott notes the verse has no counterpart in Kings and reads the 'watch of the LORD' as a watch of reverence against entering the sanctuary; Keil grounds the whole arrangement in consecration, not rank.
Henry makes it the crown of his praise of Jehoiada: 'Never let sacred things be profaned, no, not for the support of civil rights.'

themes: keeping the watch of the LORD

schools.summary: Ellicott rebuts Thenius's charge that the Chronicler turned guardsmen into Levites, proposing a combination of guard and temple-warders; Keil simply equates the Levites with the stationed guards.
Henry presses the reverence that keeps the king safe within a wall of consecrated men and the sanctuary unprofaned.

debates.question: Did the Chronicler turn the royal guardsmen into Levites to glorify the priesthood?

sides.position: Yes — a pious substitution diverting to the priesthood the honour that belonged to the Praetorians
No — Jehoiada combined the royal guard with the Levitical warders, and both really shared the day

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott explain the retained courses — the outgoing week's Levites detained to double the guard at the sabbath changeover — a shrewd, lawful muster.
Henry marvels that so many kept the secret till it was executed, fulfilling Eccl. 9:17, 'the words of the wise are heard in quiet.'

themes: the words of the wise heard in quiet

schools.summary: Ellicott notes the Chronicler's added bucklers and plural 'spears,' the arms marked by the article as David's own; Keil observes Jehoiada armed the guard from David's offerings laid up in the temple.
Clarke refers the reader to the parallel notice of the spears and bucklers at 2 Kings 11:10.

Ellicott insists 'the people' here are the armed guard, not the congregation, ranged from the right of the house to the left by the altar; Keil takes them as the Levite-guards closed into a protecting ring for the king's appearing.

themes: the armed ring around the king

schools.summary: Ellicott parses the crown (nezer) and the testimony (eduth, the law), leaving open whether the testimony was a scroll about the diadem or a law-book put in the king's hand; Keil marks the priests named as the anointers.
Clarke glosses 'God save the king' as 'May the king live!'; Wesley names Zechariah among the anointing sons whom Joash would later slay.
Henry sharpens the irony that Zechariah helped crown the man who would one day have him stoned in the temple court.

themes: the law given to the king

schools.summary: Henry sets the people's joy — a rod from the stem of Jesse — against Athaliah running upon the point of the sword of justice, deceived by the pride of her heart.
Keil frames the slaughter as in Kings and notes the Chronicler's added singers; Ellicott renders the 'noise' the queen heard as people, couriers, and acclaimers.

themes: the rod from the stem of Jesse

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the king upon his 'stand' and marks the Chronicler's characteristic addition of the Levitical musicians and 'those who taught to praise'; Keil gathers the verses under Athaliah's slaughter.
Wesley echoes the wonder of a king of David's house, a rod from the stem of Jesse long despaired of.
Henry contrasts the national gladness with the solitary fury of Athaliah, who rent her clothes while none stood with her.

themes: the promise she could not kill

schools.summary: Ellicott follows Kings closely, rendering 'have her forth of the ranges' as leading her out between the ranks and 'slay her not' as an emphatic prohibition; Keil keeps the verse in the course of the slaughter.
Clarke reads the order against her partisans as a plain measure of security for the revolution.
Henry makes the care not to slay her in the house the heart of the verse: the sacred place must not be so disgraced, nor the wicked woman so honoured.

Ellicott corrects 'laid hands on her' to 'made way for her on both sides,' the guards parting to hurry her out to the horse gate by the king's house; Keil keeps the notice as the close of the slaughter.
Clarke glosses the horse gate and refers to the parallel at 2 Kings 11:16.
Henry marks only that the sentence, once given, was done immediately.

themes: the horse gate by the king's house
made way for her on both sides

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the 'him' as the high priest representing Jehovah, avoiding the irreverence of making God a direct co-partner, and notes the omitted king-people clause on royal prerogative; Keil groups the covenant with the reforms that follow.
Clarke reads the priest as God's representative; Wesley glosses 'him' directly as the LORD, per the parallel.
Henry expounds a tripartite indenture with one intent — that they should be the LORD's people — with Jehoiada as mediator like Moses.

debates.question: Who is the 'him' of the covenant 'between him and the people and the king'?

sides.position: the high priest Jehoiada, standing as God's representative in the compact
the LORD himself, named by the pronoun, as the parallel in Kings expressly puts it

schools.summary: Henry makes the razing of Baal's house the truer half of the work — the usurper of God's right cast down as well as the usurper of the king's — grounding Mattan's death in Deut. 13.
Clarke notes the Targum's refusal to call Mattan a 'priest,' naming him only a cumera, a priestling.
Ellicott attends to the verbs of demolition and the 'thoroughly' of Kings; Keil sets the destruction as the middle term of the reformation.
Ellicott reads vv.18-19 as the Chronicler's characteristic expansion, Jehoiada restoring the Davidic courses and services neglected under Athaliah; Keil groups it with the acts of restoration.
Wesley glosses the Hebrew idiom: Jehoiada 'put the offices into the hand' of the priests and Levites, restoring them to their office.
Henry marks the two authorities — Moses for the sacrifice, David for the song — and the joy of restored worship (Rom. 5:11).

themes: Moses for sacrifice, David for song

schools.summary: Ellicott ties the porters to David's appointment and the exclusion of the unclean to the Mosaic purity laws; Keil keeps the notice in the run of restorations.
Henry reads the porters as ministers of holiness, set to keep the ceremonially unclean from the temple courts, by David's own order.

themes: reform by return to David's pattern

schools.summary: Ellicott sorts the escort — nobles and governors for the obscure Carians and couriers of Kings — and identifies the high gate with the couriers' gate; Keil keeps the enthronement in the sequence of the parallel.
Henry reads the procession as the re-establishment of civil government, the king set on the throne to rule through Jehoiada his guardian while yet a child.

themes: the king brought to the throne

schools.summary: Clarke notes the quiet city with no counter-revolution and relays the Targum's legend of the miraculous Davidic crown; Wesley reads the general joy and the quiet of the rest.
Henry (with Wesley) lifts the close into a figure of the soul: when the Son of David is enthroned, all within is quiet and springs of joy are opened.
Keil lets the notice stand as the settled end of the account, the rest that follows Athaliah's removal.

outliers.note: Relays the Targum's legend of the miraculous Davidic crown — taken from the Ammonite king, set with a loadstone engraven with the divine Name and weighing a talent of gold, which none but David's seed could bear — reported, not adopted, as a witness to the conviction that the throne belonged to David's line alone.
